```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/common.R")
panel <- read.csv("data/vendor_panel.csv")
```

## The decision problem

Your bank pays a vendor for a number. Every month, a model called VendorScore hands
NorthPoint Bank a risk score for each of its `r length(unique(panel$vendor_id))` third-party
vendors. Nobody at the bank can see the code, the training data, or the method. The
scores arrive, and decisions follow.

How do you validate something you cannot open? This series shows how much can be learned
from the scores and what happens afterwards, and where outside testing stops.

## The three questions

The April 17, 2026 interagency [*Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management*](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13a.pdf)
(Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) is explicitly non-prescriptive. We read it as describing sound
practice, not rules. The three questions below are this project's practical interpretation,
not a regulator-prescribed checklist. Each works on any risk model.

1. **Are its probabilities honest?** When the model says 10%, do incidents happen about 10%
   of the time? This is calibration, tested with [`probcal`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=probcal) ([Page 2](calibration.qmd)).
2. **Does it beat a simple model?** A sophisticated model should outperform a plain
   12-month average, and keep doing so when conditions change. This is forecast dominance,
   tested with [`forecastdom`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=forecastdom) ([Page 3](forecast.qmd)).
3. **Would its headline finding survive a push?** Some findings collapse under a small
   change of method or data. This is fragility, tested with [`falsifyr`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=falsifyr) ([Page 4](fragility.qmd)).

![Each test is tied to a question and to the decision it protects.](figures/three_questions.svg){#fig-overview fig-alt="Three panels. Calibration asks whether probabilities are honest. Forecast dominance asks whether the model beats a simple one. Fragility asks whether the headline survives a push."}

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Each of the three columns is one question. Reading down a
column, you see the question, the test used to answer it, and the decision that test
protects.

**What the plot tells you.** A model can pass one test and fail another, so one test
alone leaves two decisions unprotected.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Materiality box (illustrative ratings)

Judging how much validation a model deserves (guidance §III) looks at three things:

- **Inherent risk: high.** VendorScore is opaque, its assumptions and data are hidden, and
  vendor incidents are rare events, which limits the data available to test it.
- **Exposure: broad.** The score covers all `r length(unique(panel$vendor_id))` vendors in the portfolio.
- **Purpose: consequential.** Scores inform monitoring intensity and contract terms.

Exposure and purpose together determine materiality, assessed alongside inherent risk.
Illustrative conclusion: full validation is warranted.
:::

## The case

NorthPoint Bank is a fictional regional bank with about $45 billion in assets. The
guidance is expected to be most relevant to banks above $30 billion; some smaller banks may
also find it relevant. Asset managers and fintechs fall outside its scope but can adopt
similar practices voluntarily.

All four pages share one synthetic dataset: `r format(nrow(panel), big.mark = ",")` vendor-months (300 vendors over
48 months, January 2022 to December 2025), with `r sum(panel$incident)` observed incidents,
or `r pct(mean(panel$incident), 2)` of vendor-months. Because the data are simulated, we know each
vendor-month's true incident probability and use it only as a reference. The models under
test never see it. Everything is reproducible from seed 34.

A fictional vendor, RiskMetric Systems, supplies VendorScore, trained on months 1 to 30.
NorthPoint fits a recalibration overlay on months 31 to 36 and assesses it on months 37 to
48 (Page 2). Page 3 compares the raw scores with a benchmark over months 31 to 48, a
period that includes a deterioration in vendors' patching speed after month 36.

## The black-box problem

Guidance on vendor products (§VII) recognises that a bank may lack access to a vendor
model's inner workings. The vendor's summary offers only "ensemble machine learning on
proprietary threat intelligence," an AUC of 0.81 "on vendor development data," and the
assertion that scores are "well-calibrated."

The bank can evaluate how the scores perform on its own outcomes, for calibration and
discrimination. It cannot reproduce the vendor's development-data AUC or inspect the
hidden development choices. Testing scores against outcomes is partial validation only: it
cannot confirm that the proprietary model is conceptually sound. That depends on what the
vendor discloses (§VII).

## How to read this series

Pages 2 to 4 share one structure: the question, the method in brief, the findings, what
they mean for the bank, and one committee action phrased as "sound practice suggests…".
The expected findings were written as hypotheses before any analysis ran; where a result
differs, the text reports the result. Code is folded by default. Page 4 closes with a
scorecard of measured results; a final page covers reproducibility and limits.
